text:
Psychological First Aid: The First Five Minutes

Anything that could let someone hurt themselves in the next five minutes takes priority, so get the car keys out of reach and turn the stove off, and move them away from roads and balconies, or pools of water for that matter. Letting them move around is fine, and pacing can help, but keep them from taking more of any substance. If they want to go confront somebody, that can wait. And if they want to leave, have someone go with them. Put any weapons away and keep the person away from crowds and strangers. If they want to post their big revelation about the universe, or message an ex, take the phone.

They're feeling overwhelmed, so dim the lights, and clear out the extra people around them.

Then remind them where they are and what's happening, since a trip can make them lose track of it:

You're in [place]. It's [date/time]. You took [substance, if known], and its effects will peak and then change.

After the Storm

Once you've slept, write down what happened while it's still fresh: what you took and roughly how much, where you were, who was around, and what made it better or worse. Then go through it piece by piece. Maybe the panic hit right when the cannabis did, or right when the room got crowded. Maybe part of it was grief you've been carrying for years, or an old trauma. And maybe the part that felt like prophecy at 3 a.m. was a fantasy. Notice what was useful, and what you've already started doing differently. Some of it might call for therapy or an apology, some just for a long rest. And some of it is as plain as finding a better sitter, or keeping a bottle of water within reach next time.

It can feel like the more cosmic the story sounds, the bigger the insight. But the fruit of an insight is whether suffering goes down and love gets more available.

questions.Q1: PASS: each new paragraph opens on its point: the first don't (no arguing with visions); write down the facts once slept; what CBT's distortions are and what they do; plan the start and the end before taking anything
questions.Q2: PASS: every act is the reader's own or the helper's, with its purpose; the distortions are what the reader's own mind does
questions.Q3: PASS: which things exactly: the being in the corner, a memory that came back, eye contact, touch, music, prayer, chanting; what you took and how much, the cannabis, the crowded room, grief, prophecy at 3 a.m., a better sitter, a bottle of water; each distortion's own words; the substance and dose, what it mixes badly with, the room, food, company and sleep
questions.Q4: PASS: the fresh reader's unclear terms (sense/SENSE-READ.md) answered in their sentences: the sitter is the sober person with you, cognitive distortions are the ways a frightened mind twists what it sees, low-directivity support is keeping you safe and offering choices, and 'return to the room and date' is checking where you are and what day it is; 'failing the medicine' stays, as the label a ceremony might put on a tripper
questions.Q5: PASS: each turn has what it turns on: 'But' for the limit on not arguing, 'then' for the steps, 'and maybe' for the last kind of thing found, 'because' for keeping the day free
questions.Q6: PASS: in the reader's order: the don'ts, then what to say instead; write, then sort, then what follows; the distortions one by one; before, during, the end, after
questions.Q7: PASS: every fact is about the person in front of them, or their own session
questions.Q8: PASS: each new part is its section's one point, under its heading
questions.Q9: PASS: nothing compressed: each list taken apart into sentences, an item or a pair each, with the small words that carry the relations ('but', 'then', 'and maybe', 'because')

question_text.Q1: Why am I reading this sentence, and do I know it before I have to work through it? (the point first, in each sentence and each paragraph; a study after the question it answers; a term explained where it is first used, never in a sentence after it)
question_text.Q2: What is each instruction for, said in the reader's terms, and is it something the helper does ("have someone go with them"), not a rule stated as a fact ("someone goes with them")?
question_text.Q3: Which thing exactly? (pools of water, not water; any substance, not anything)
question_text.Q4: What does each word act on, or mean here? (adjunct remedy; known-genuine) Is every term a high-school graduate wouldn't know (enterocytes, BPC-157) explained once, where it is first used, and common ones (a vitamin) left alone? Is each mechanism explained by what it does in the reader's experience (dopamine "for motivation (by showing us what is important to pay attention to)"; DeltaFosB "preventing that learning from really clicking"), not by where it sits or what it looks like ("a chemical blanket", "the slower one underneath")? (E375)
question_text.Q5: Why does each sentence follow from the one before? (every but, so, because and this has what it turns on)
question_text.Q6: Is this the order the reader is thinking in, and does each idea sit next to what it continues?
question_text.Q7: Does each fact help this reader now, in their case (the same kind of thing they face, not just the same topic)?
question_text.Q8: Does each item belong in the group it is put in?
question_text.Q9: Is anything compressed? (one step a sentence, the small words that carry the relation, no space before mg)
